questions.topic: Prompt Building Blocks (Role, Context, Task, Constraint, Format)

questions.topic: Prompt Building Blocks (Role, Context, Task, Constraint, Format)
questions.question: A prompt says only: 'Write a report.' What is the most likely problem with this prompt?

options.A: There is no problem; short prompts always work best
options.B: It is too long
options.C: It omits nearly all the building blocks — no context, no specific task detail, no constraints, no format — so Claude has to guess at what's actually needed
options.D: It uses too many technical terms

questions.explanation: Missing context, specifics, constraints, and format forces guesswork and produces a generic, likely unusable result.

questions.topic: Prompt Building Blocks (Role, Context, Task, Constraint, Format)
questions.question: Which addition would most improve the prompt 'Summarize this document' for a business user who needs it for a specific purpose?

options.A: Adding more punctuation

options.C: Specifying the audience, desired length, and what the summary will be used for (e.g., 'for an executive who needs 3 bullet points to decide whether to approve the budget')
options.D: Removing the word 'document'

questions.explanation: Clarifying audience, length, and purpose turns a vague request into one Claude can target precisely.

questions.topic: Prompt Building Blocks (Role, Context, Task, Constraint, Format)
questions.question: In prompt design, what does the 'constraint' building block typically refer to?

options.A: The model's maximum context window size
options.B: A password required to access Claude
options.C: The number of people who can view the output
options.D: Limits the user sets on the output, such as length, tone, or things to avoid

questions.explanation: Constraints are user-specified limits — length, tone, style, things to include or avoid — that shape the output.

questions.topic: Prompt Building Blocks (Role, Context, Task, Constraint, Format)
questions.question: A user wants a prompt that reliably produces output formatted as a numbered list of action items with owners and due dates. What should the prompt explicitly specify?

options.A: Nothing beyond the topic; Claude will always guess the right format
options.B: The exact output format wanted (numbered list, with owner and due date fields for each item)
options.C: Only the tone
options.D: Only the audience

questions.explanation: Specifying the exact output format is the most direct way to reliably get a structured list rather than free-flowing prose.

questions.topic: Prompt Building Blocks (Role, Context, Task, Constraint, Format)

options.D: Providing context always makes responses slower with no benefit

questions.topic: Prompt Building Blocks (Role, Context, Task, Constraint, Format)
questions.question: A user asks Claude to 'write a project update' without further detail, gets a generic response, and is unsatisfied. What is the most likely root cause?

options.C: Claude is malfunctioning
options.D: The prompt lacked context, task specifics, constraints, and format guidance, leaving Claude to guess at what a 'good' update looks like

questions.explanation: A generic prompt without the building blocks predictably yields a generic response — this is a prompting issue, not a tool failure.

questions.topic: Prompt Building Blocks (Role, Context, Task, Constraint, Format)
questions.question: What risk does omitting the 'format' building block create, even when role, context, and task are all well specified?

options.A: No risk; format never matters if the content is good

options.C: Claude may return the right content in a format that doesn't fit how the output will actually be used, requiring rework
options.D: Format only matters for coding tasks

questions.explanation: Even excellent content can require rework if it arrives in the wrong shape for its intended use.

questions.topic: Prompt Building Blocks (Role, Context, Task, Constraint, Format)
questions.question: A marketing associate needs a prompt for turning bullet-point notes into a polished LinkedIn post. Which detail is LEAST important to include?

options.A: The core message or notes to turn into the post
options.B: A rough character/length limit matching LinkedIn norms
options.C: The target audience and desired tone
options.D: The exact font the final post should display in

questions.explanation: Font is a rendering detail outside Claude's control for a text response; audience, tone, length, and source content actually shape a useful draft.

questions.topic: Task Decomposition (Breaking Big Requests into Steps)
questions.question: Why is breaking a large, complex request into smaller steps generally more effective than asking for everything at once?

options.A: It never actually helps; one large prompt is always equivalent
options.B: Smaller steps let you review and correct each stage before building on it, reducing the chance an early misunderstanding propagates through the final output
options.C: Breaking tasks into steps only matters for coding
options.D: It exists purely to increase token usage

questions.explanation: Reviewing intermediate steps catches misunderstandings early, before they compound into a flawed final deliverable.

questions.topic: Task Decomposition (Breaking Big Requests into Steps)
questions.question: A user needs a full market-entry analysis covering competitors, pricing, and a go/no-go recommendation. What is a better approach than one giant prompt?

options.A: Ask for the entire analysis in one shot and hope it's coherent
options.B: Break it into stages — competitor research, then pricing analysis, then synthesize into a recommendation — reviewing each stage before moving on
options.C: There is no better approach; decomposition doesn't help with analysis tasks
options.D: Ask Claude to guess which parts matter most and skip the rest

questions.explanation: Staged decomposition lets you validate each component before the final synthesis depends on it.

questions.topic: Task Decomposition (Breaking Big Requests into Steps)
questions.question: Which task is the best candidate for decomposition into multiple smaller prompts?

options.A: Fixing a single typo in a sentence
options.B: Asking for a one-word yes/no answer
options.C: Asking for today's date
options.D: Producing a 40-page vendor evaluation report covering multiple vendors, criteria, and a final recommendation

questions.explanation: Large, multi-part deliverables with dependent stages benefit most from decomposition.

questions.topic: Task Decomposition (Breaking Big Requests into Steps)
questions.question: What is a reasonable way to decompose the task 'create a full onboarding plan for new hires'?

options.A: Ask a completely unrelated question first
options.B: Ask for the entire plan in a single unstructured request
options.C: Decomposition is unnecessary for planning tasks
options.D: First outline the key phases, then develop each phase's content in turn, reviewing as you go

questions.explanation: Outlining phases first, then filling in each phase, is a natural staged decomposition that keeps each step reviewable.

questions.topic: Task Decomposition (Breaking Big Requests into Steps)
questions.question: After asking Claude to outline a report's structure, what is the most effective next step before requesting the full draft?

options.A: Ask an unrelated question to test Claude's general knowledge
options.B: Immediately ask for the full draft with no review of the outline
options.C: Start over from scratch with an unrelated prompt
options.D: Review and adjust the outline so the foundation is right before the larger draft is built on top of it

questions.explanation: Validating the outline before drafting prevents structural problems from propagating into a much larger piece of work.

questions.topic: Task Decomposition (Breaking Big Requests into Steps)
questions.question: What is a key risk of NOT decomposing a very large, multi-part request?

options.A: Large requests are processed identically regardless of decomposition
options.B: There is no risk; large single requests always work equally well
options.C: A single misunderstanding early in a long response can propagate through the rest of the output, and errors may be harder to spot
options.D: Decomposition always produces worse results than one large prompt

questions.explanation: Errors are easier to catch and fix when surfaced at each stage rather than buried inside one long, undifferentiated response.

questions.topic: Task Decomposition (Breaking Big Requests into Steps)
questions.question: A user wants Claude to research a topic, draft an article, and then format it for a newsletter. What is a sound decomposition of this request?

options.A: Separate steps: gather the research, then draft the article from that material, then reformat the approved draft for the newsletter
options.B: Skip research and go straight to formatting
options.C: Ask for the newsletter format before any content exists
options.D: One single prompt combining research, drafting, and formatting instructions with no intermediate checkpoints

questions.explanation: Sequencing research, then drafting, then formatting lets each stage build on a validated version of the previous one.

questions.topic: Task Decomposition (Breaking Big Requests into Steps)
questions.question: A user decomposes a task into five sequential prompts but doesn't review any intermediate output before issuing the next prompt. What have they lost, compared to true staged decomposition?

options.A: Sequential prompting without review is always faster and equally reliable
options.B: Nothing; issuing the prompts in sequence is sufficient regardless of review
options.C: The main benefit of decomposition — catching and correcting errors at each stage before they propagate
options.D: This approach guarantees a better result than a single combined prompt

questions.explanation: Decomposition's value comes specifically from the review-and-correct opportunity between steps; skipping review forfeits that benefit.

questions.topic: Task Decomposition (Breaking Big Requests into Steps)
questions.question: Which best describes when task decomposition is LEAST necessary?

options.A: For a short, simple, single-part request with a clear, low-stakes answer
options.B: For a lengthy, multi-stage deliverable with dependencies between sections
options.C: For any request involving more than one sentence
options.D: Decomposition is always necessary regardless of task size

questions.explanation: Simple, low-stakes, single-part requests don't have the dependency chains that make decomposition valuable.

questions.topic: Task Decomposition (Breaking Big Requests into Steps)
questions.question: A user asks for a 'complete competitive analysis, financial model, and go-to-market plan' in one prompt. What is a likely downside of this all-at-once approach?

options.A: Quality across all three deliverables may suffer, and errors in one section are harder to isolate and fix without affecting the others
options.B: Combining requests always improves coherence with no downside
options.C: No downside; combining unrelated deliverables into one prompt is always optimal
options.D: This approach is guaranteed to be faster with no quality tradeoff

questions.explanation: Bundling several substantial, loosely related deliverables into one request makes it harder to isolate and fix problems in any single component.

questions.topic: Iterative Prompt Refinement (Diagnosing and Improving Weak Prompts)
questions.question: When a first response from Claude falls short, what is generally the most effective next step?

options.A: Give up on the task entirely
options.B: Diagnose specifically what's missing or wrong, then give a targeted follow-up instruction addressing that specific gap
options.C: Repeat the identical prompt verbatim and hope for a different result
options.D: Switch to writing the entire deliverable by hand with no further use of Claude

questions.explanation: Specific, targeted feedback about what's actually wrong is far more effective than vague dissatisfaction or blind repetition.

questions.topic: Iterative Prompt Refinement (Diagnosing and Improving Weak Prompts)
questions.question: A user receives a draft that is 'too long and too formal.' Which follow-up is most likely to produce an improved result?

options.A: 'This is bad, try again.'
options.B: 'Cut this to about half the length and make the tone more conversational — imagine explaining it to a colleague over coffee.'
options.C: Simply resend the exact same original prompt
options.D: 'Fix it.'

questions.explanation: Naming the specific problems and the specific desired direction gives Claude concrete, actionable feedback.

questions.topic: Iterative Prompt Refinement (Diagnosing and Improving Weak Prompts)
questions.question: What is the value of a structured diagnosis (what's wrong, why, what specific change would fix it) before giving feedback to Claude?

options.A: It only helps with coding tasks
options.B: It has no value; any vague feedback works equally well
options.C: It turns a vague reaction into an actionable instruction Claude can act on directly, rather than leaving Claude to guess what changed
options.D: It guarantees a perfect result on the very next attempt

questions.explanation: Concrete, diagnosed feedback removes the guesswork that vague dissatisfaction leaves for the next attempt.

questions.topic: Iterative Prompt Refinement (Diagnosing and Improving Weak Prompts)
questions.question: A response nails the content but uses jargon the intended audience won't understand. What is the most precise refinement instruction?

options.A: 'Make it better.'
options.B: 'This is wrong.'
options.C: 'Rewrite this for someone with no background in the subject — replace technical terms with plain-language explanations.'
options.D: Resend the exact same prompt

questions.explanation: Naming the specific issue and the specific fix is the actionable refinement.

questions.topic: Iterative Prompt Refinement (Diagnosing and Improving Weak Prompts)
questions.question: Which feedback is an example of vague, low-value feedback that Claude cannot act on precisely?

options.A: 'This isn't quite right.'
options.B: 'The second paragraph repeats the first point — please remove the repetition.'
options.C: 'Replace the word "leverage" with "use" throughout.'
options.D: 'Shorten the introduction to two sentences.'

questions.explanation: 'This isn't quite right' gives no specific, actionable direction, unlike the other options.

questions.topic: Iterative Prompt Refinement (Diagnosing and Improving Weak Prompts)
questions.question: Why is reissuing the exact same prompt after an unsatisfactory response usually ineffective?

options.A: It is always effective and guaranteed to fix the issue
options.B: Resending prompts is technically impossible
options.C: Claude only allows a prompt to be sent once
options.D: Without new information about what specifically needs to change, there's little reason to expect a meaningfully different or better result

questions.explanation: Without added or corrected information, there's no new signal to change the outcome meaningfully.

questions.topic: Iterative Prompt Refinement (Diagnosing and Improving Weak Prompts)
questions.question: A user isn't sure exactly what's wrong with a response, only that 'something feels off.' What is a productive way to proceed?

options.A: Ask Claude to explain its reasoning or assumptions for the parts that feel off, which can surface the specific issue and inform a targeted fix
options.B: Repeat the same prompt with no changes
options.C: Give up and write the whole thing manually
options.D: Assume the response is fine despite the discomfort

questions.explanation: Prompting Claude to surface its reasoning/assumptions can help pinpoint vague discomfort into something specific and fixable.

questions.topic: Iterative Prompt Refinement (Diagnosing and Improving Weak Prompts)
questions.question: A draft correctly follows every instruction given, but the user is unsatisfied because an important requirement was never actually stated. What is the real issue here?

options.A: The original prompt was incomplete — the missing requirement needs to be added explicitly in a follow-up
options.B: Claude made an error that needs correcting
options.C: The user should abandon the task
options.D: This situation is impossible

questions.explanation: If an unstated requirement wasn't met, that's a prompting gap to fill in, not necessarily a model mistake.

questions.topic: Iterative Prompt Refinement (Diagnosing and Improving Weak Prompts)
questions.question: What is the benefit of iterating in small, targeted steps versus bundling many unrelated changes into one revision request?

options.A: Bundling changes is always faster with no tradeoff
options.B: Targeted iteration is only relevant for coding tasks
options.C: It's easier to verify each specific change worked, and to isolate the source if the revision introduces a new problem
options.D: There is no benefit; bundling is always equally effective

questions.explanation: Isolating changes makes it easier to confirm each fix worked and trace any new issue back to its source.

questions.topic: Iterative Prompt Refinement (Diagnosing and Improving Weak Prompts)
questions.question: After three rounds of revision, a draft still misses the mark in the same way each time. What does this suggest?

options.A: Nothing; this is expected and unrelated to feedback quality
options.B: Claude is incapable of ever producing a correct response
options.C: The task should be abandoned permanently
options.D: The feedback given may not be specifically targeting the actual root issue, and it's worth re-diagnosing the problem more precisely

questions.explanation: A repeated, unresolved issue across multiple rounds signals a need to re-diagnose the actual root cause.

questions.topic: Task-Type Prompting Strategies (Analysis, Research, Drafting, Brainstorming)
questions.question: For a brainstorming task where the goal is a wide variety of creative ideas, which prompting approach is most effective?

options.A: Ask for exactly one 'correct' idea and stop
options.B: Avoid giving any topic at all
options.C: Constrain the response to a single rigid format with no room for variation
options.D: Explicitly ask for a large number of diverse ideas, encourage unconventional options, and defer judging quality until after generation

questions.explanation: Brainstorming benefits from explicitly requesting volume and diversity, and separating idea generation from evaluation.

options.A: The user's favorite color
options.B: What sources or materials to draw from, and what specific questions the summary needs to answer
options.C: The exact time of day the request was made
options.D: Nothing beyond the topic name

questions.topic: Task-Type Prompting Strategies (Analysis, Research, Drafting, Brainstorming)
questions.question: For a drafting task (e.g., writing a formal proposal), which prompting detail matters most beyond the core content?

options.A: Audience, tone, and structural conventions expected for that document type
options.B: The exact number of times the word 'the' should appear
options.C: Nothing; drafting tasks need no additional detail beyond the topic
options.D: The user's internal task-tracking ID

questions.explanation: Audience, tone, and structural/genre conventions most directly shape whether a draft reads appropriately for its purpose.

questions.topic: Task-Type Prompting Strategies (Analysis, Research, Drafting, Brainstorming)
questions.question: A user needs Claude to analyze a dataset summary and identify trends. Which prompting element is most critical?

options.A: A request for creative flourishes and metaphors
options.B: Clarity about which specific questions or comparisons the analysis should address
options.C: No specifics at all beyond 'analyze this'
options.D: A request for the longest possible response

questions.explanation: Analytical tasks benefit from specific, targeted questions rather than an open-ended 'analyze this' with no direction.

questions.topic: Task-Type Prompting Strategies (Analysis, Research, Drafting, Brainstorming)
questions.question: Why might the same prompting principles need to be applied differently for a brainstorming task versus a drafting task?

options.A: They don't need to be applied differently at all
options.B: Brainstorming benefits from loosening constraints to encourage volume/variety, while drafting benefits from tighter constraints to produce a usable, polished result
options.C: Brainstorming should always have the strictest constraints of any task type
options.D: Task type has no bearing on how constraints should be set

questions.explanation: The right balance of constraint vs. openness shifts with the task's goal.

questions.topic: Task-Type Prompting Strategies (Analysis, Research, Drafting, Brainstorming)
questions.question: A user brainstorming names for a new product gets ten very similar, safe suggestions. What prompt adjustment would likely produce more variety?

options.A: Ask for the exact same prompt again with no changes
options.B: Explicitly ask for a wider range, including some bold or unconventional options, grouped by different themes or angles
options.C: Reduce the number of ideas requested
options.D: Remove all context about the product

questions.explanation: Directly asking for range, unconventional options, or varied angles counteracts a tendency toward safe, similar suggestions.

questions.topic: Task-Type Prompting Strategies (Analysis, Research, Drafting, Brainstorming)
questions.question: For a research task requiring up-to-date facts, which caveat is most important for the user to keep in mind?

options.A: None; all information Claude provides is always guaranteed current and correct
options.B: Claude's knowledge may not reflect the most recent developments unless using a feature designed for current information, so time-sensitive facts should be verified
options.C: Research tasks should never be attempted with AI assistance
options.D: Research tasks require no verification of any kind

questions.explanation: Recognizing the limits of static knowledge and verifying time-sensitive claims is central to responsible research use.

questions.topic: Task-Type Prompting Strategies (Analysis, Research, Drafting, Brainstorming)
questions.question: Which is the best prompting approach for drafting a formal client-facing letter versus an internal quick-note?

options.A: Specify a more formal tone and careful structure for the client letter, while allowing a more casual, abbreviated style for the internal note
options.B: Always default to the most formal tone regardless of audience
options.C: Always default to the most casual tone regardless of audience
options.D: Use identical instructions for both; formality never needs to be specified

questions.explanation: Matching tone and structure to the audience and stakes of each document type is a core task-type prompting adjustment.

questions.topic: Task-Type Prompting Strategies (Analysis, Research, Drafting, Brainstorming)
questions.question: What distinguishes an 'analysis' task from a 'drafting' task in terms of prompting needs?

options.A: Drafting tasks never need any context
options.B: There is no meaningful distinction
options.C: Analysis tasks need clear evaluative questions/criteria; drafting tasks need clear tone, structure, and audience guidance
options.D: Analysis tasks never need any context

questions.explanation: Each task type has different success criteria, shifting the prompting emphasis accordingly.

questions.topic: Task-Type Prompting Strategies (Analysis, Research, Drafting, Brainstorming)
questions.question: A user wants both a brainstorm of options AND a recommendation of the best one. What is a sound way to structure this request?

options.A: Skip the brainstorm entirely and ask only for one final answer
options.B: There is no reasonable way to combine these two goals
options.C: First request a wide brainstorm without judgment, then in a follow-up ask Claude to evaluate the list and recommend the strongest option against stated criteria
options.D: Ask for both simultaneously with no separation, and hope the two goals don't interfere

questions.explanation: Separating divergent brainstorming from convergent evaluation avoids one goal narrowing the other prematurely.

questions.topic: Task-Type Prompting Strategies (Analysis, Research, Drafting, Brainstorming)
questions.question: Which is a reasonable adaptation when a research summary needs to serve a non-expert executive audience rather than a technical team?

options.A: Emphasize implications and recommendations over technical detail, and define or avoid jargon the executive audience won't need

options.C: Add more technical jargon to seem more credible
options.D: No adaptation needed; the same summary works for every audience

questions.explanation: Tailoring depth, jargon, and emphasis to the audience's needs is central to adapting a summary for a different reader.

questions.topic: Task-Type Prompting Strategies (Analysis, Research, Drafting, Brainstorming)
questions.question: Why is it useful to explicitly tell Claude which task type you're aiming for (e.g., 'this is a brainstorm, not a final decision')?

options.C: It only matters for very long documents
options.D: Task type framing is only relevant in coding contexts

questions.explanation: Naming the task type helps Claude calibrate whether to prioritize breadth/creativity or precision/finality.

questions.topic: Encouraging Creative and Divergent Output

options.D: Requesting the shortest possible response

questions.explanation: Explicitly inviting unconventional ideas up front, with feasibility filtering deferred, tends to widen the range generated.

questions.question: Why might separating 'idea generation' from 'idea evaluation' into two distinct steps improve brainstorming quality?

questions.topic: Hallucination Detection (Fabricated Facts and Plausible-Looking Errors)

options.B: They are the same activity with no meaningful difference
options.C: Fact-checking involves actively comparing specific claims against an independent, authoritative source, not just assessing whether the response reads plausibly
options.D: Careful reading is always sufficient and fact-checking is unnecessary

questions.explanation: Careful reading assesses internal plausibility; fact-checking requires an external, independent comparison point.

questions.topic: Fact-Checking Against Primary Sources
questions.question: A user finds that a primary source contradicts a specific claim in Claude's response. What is the correct next step?

options.A: Correct the claim in the deliverable to match the verified primary source
options.B: Ignore the contradiction since the AI response sounded confident
options.C: Include both contradictory versions with no resolution
options.D: Trust the AI-generated claim over the primary source

questions.explanation: When a verified primary source contradicts an AI claim, the primary source should take precedence in the final deliverable.

questions.topic: Fact-Checking Against Primary Sources
questions.question: Which of these is the best example of a primary source for a claim about a company's quarterly revenue?

options.A: The company's own official quarterly financial filing or earnings release
options.B: An AI-generated estimate with no cited source
options.C: A blog post summarizing 'some recent news about the company'
options.D: A rumor shared on an online forum

questions.explanation: The company's own official filing or earnings release is the authoritative primary source for its reported revenue.

questions.topic: Fact-Checking Against Primary Sources
questions.question: A user is preparing a client-facing document citing an industry statistic. What is the strongest verification practice?

options.A: Use the AI-generated statistic as-is, since it sounds authoritative
options.B: Locate the original study or dataset behind the statistic and confirm the number and its context (e.g., sample size, year) match what's being claimed
options.C: Change the statistic slightly so it can't be checked
options.D: Remove all numbers from the document to avoid the issue entirely

questions.explanation: Tracing to the original study/dataset and confirming both the number and its context is the thorough, correct verification approach.

questions.topic: Fact-Checking Against Primary Sources
questions.question: Why might checking 'context' (e.g., sample size, date, scope) matter as much as checking the raw number itself when fact-checking a statistic?

options.A: Numbers are always self-explanatory with no need for context
options.B: Context checking is only relevant for scientific papers
options.C: Context never matters; only the raw number needs checking
options.D: A technically correct number can still be misleading if its context (e.g., a tiny sample size or an outdated date) isn't accurately represented

questions.explanation: A correct number with missing or misrepresented context can still lead to a misleading conclusion, so context is part of a complete fact-check.

questions.topic: Fact-Checking Against Primary Sources
questions.question: A draft states a fact 'according to a well-known study,' with no further detail. What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Accept the vague attribution as sufficient sourcing
options.B: Ask for or independently find the specific study being referenced, and verify the claim directly against it
options.C: Assume 'well-known' means verification is unnecessary
options.D: Remove the word 'study' but keep the unverified claim

questions.explanation: A vague attribution like 'a well-known study' isn't a real, checkable source — the specific study needs to be identified and checked directly.

questions.topic: Fact-Checking Against Primary Sources
questions.question: What is a practical benefit of building a habit of checking primary sources for high-stakes claims, even when a claim seems obviously true?

options.A: It catches the occasional subtly wrong or outdated 'obvious' fact before it causes real harm, and reinforces a consistent, disciplined verification habit
options.B: There is no benefit; obviously true claims never need checking
options.C: It always slows down work with no offsetting benefit
options.D: It is only useful for claims that seem obviously false

questions.explanation: Consistent verification habits catch the rare but costly cases where an 'obvious' fact turns out to be subtly wrong or outdated.

questions.topic: Fact-Checking Against Primary Sources
questions.question: A user needs to verify a claim about a competitor's product feature. Which is the strongest source to check?

options.A: An anonymous online comment about the competitor
options.B: The competitor's own official product documentation or website
options.C: The AI response's own restated confidence
options.D: A completely unrelated company's documentation

questions.explanation: The competitor's own official documentation is the authoritative primary source for claims about their product's actual features.

questions.topic: Structural and Logical Consistency Evaluation
questions.question: What does evaluating a document's 'internal consistency' mean?

options.A: Checking whether the document uses a consistent font
options.B: Checking whether claims, numbers, and conclusions in different parts of the document agree with each other rather than contradicting one another
options.C: Checking whether the document was written quickly
options.D: Checking whether the document matches a competitor's document

questions.explanation: Internal consistency means the document doesn't contradict itself across its own sections, numbers, or conclusions.

questions.topic: Structural and Logical Consistency Evaluation
questions.question: A report's executive summary states a recommendation that isn't actually supported by the analysis in the body of the report. What kind of problem is this?

options.A: A formatting-only issue unrelated to content quality
options.B: A minor stylistic issue with no real impact
options.C: A structural/logical consistency problem — the conclusion doesn't follow from the presented evidence, and this should be caught before the report is finalized
options.D: This is not a real problem worth checking for

questions.explanation: A conclusion unsupported by the body's evidence is a genuine logical-consistency flaw, not a cosmetic issue.

questions.topic: Structural and Logical Consistency Evaluation
questions.question: Why is checking a document's overall logical flow important, even if each individual sentence is well-written?

options.A: Logical flow is irrelevant to document quality
options.B: Individual sentence quality guarantees the document as a whole makes sense
options.C: This only matters for creative writing, not business documents
options.D: Well-written individual sentences can still fail to build toward a coherent overall argument or structure if the flow between them isn't checked

questions.explanation: Sentence-level polish doesn't guarantee document-level coherence — the overall argument structure needs separate evaluation.

questions.topic: Structural and Logical Consistency Evaluation
questions.question: A proposal recommends 'Option A' in its conclusion but the comparison table earlier in the document shows 'Option B' scoring higher on every criterion. What should a careful reviewer do?

options.A: Ignore the discrepancy since the writing quality is otherwise good
options.B: Publish both conflicting conclusions and let the reader decide
options.C: Flag the inconsistency and resolve it — either correct the recommendation or correct the comparison table — before finalizing the document
options.D: Delete the comparison table to hide the discrepancy

questions.explanation: A direct contradiction between the supporting data and the stated conclusion must be resolved, not published or ignored.

questions.topic: Structural and Logical Consistency Evaluation
questions.question: What does 'audience suitability' mean when evaluating a document's structure?

options.A: Whether the document uses the reader's preferred font
options.B: Whether the content's depth, tone, and structure are appropriate for who will actually be reading and using the document
options.C: Whether the document is the correct file size
options.D: Whether the document was proofread for spelling only

questions.explanation: Audience suitability is about matching depth, tone, and structure to the actual reader's needs and expertise level.

questions.topic: Structural and Logical Consistency Evaluation
questions.question: A technical document intended for a general business audience is full of unexplained jargon and deep technical detail. What evaluation issue does this represent?

options.A: No issue; more detail is always better regardless of audience
options.B: A purely cosmetic issue unrelated to the document's usefulness
options.C: This is only a problem if the reader explicitly complains
options.D: A mismatch between the document's structure/content and its intended audience, which should be flagged and revised before distribution

questions.explanation: Content that doesn't match the audience's background undermines the document's usefulness, regardless of technical accuracy.

questions.topic: Structural and Logical Consistency Evaluation
questions.question: Which of these is an example of a structural (not factual) problem in a document?

options.A: A statistic that is factually wrong
options.B: A conclusion section that doesn't logically follow from the evidence presented earlier in the same document
options.C: A citation that cannot be found in any source
options.D: A quote that was never actually said

questions.explanation: A conclusion misaligned with its own supporting evidence is a structural/logical flaw, distinct from a factual accuracy error.

questions.topic: Structural and Logical Consistency Evaluation
questions.question: A user reviewing a long report notices that terminology for the same concept changes partway through (e.g., 'client' becomes 'customer' with no explanation). What should happen?

options.A: Nothing; inconsistent terminology never affects clarity
options.B: The terminology should be standardized throughout the document for clarity and professionalism, since inconsistent terms can confuse readers
options.C: This is a factual error requiring source verification
options.D: The document should be rejected entirely and never revised

questions.explanation: Inconsistent terminology is a structural/clarity issue that should simply be standardized during review, not treated as a fatal flaw or a factual error.

questions.topic: Structural and Logical Consistency Evaluation
questions.question: Why should a reviewer check whether a document's sections are logically ordered, not just individually well-written?

options.A: Section order never affects how well a document communicates
options.B: A logical, well-ordered flow (e.g., background before analysis before recommendation) helps the reader follow and be persuaded by the argument, regardless of individual sentence quality
options.C: Order only matters for creative writing
options.D: Documents should always be ordered alphabetically by section name

questions.explanation: A logical section order supports the reader's ability to follow and be persuaded by the overall argument.

questions.topic: Structural and Logical Consistency Evaluation
questions.question: A document intended to persuade a skeptical audience presents its recommendation first, with supporting evidence buried at the very end. What structural improvement would likely help?

options.A: Reordering to build the case with evidence before the recommendation (or otherwise ensuring the skeptical reader sees the reasoning before being asked to accept the conclusion)
options.B: Removing all evidence entirely to shorten the document
options.C: No change needed; order never affects persuasiveness
options.D: Repeating the recommendation multiple times instead of adding evidence

questions.explanation: For a skeptical audience, evidence-before-conclusion structuring is generally more persuasive than leading with an unsupported claim.

questions.topic: Structural and Logical Consistency Evaluation
questions.question: What is a reasonable check for whether a document's claims are appropriately supported?

options.A: Assume all claims are supported if the document is long enough
options.B: Verify that each significant claim has either explicit supporting evidence/reasoning in the document or a cited source, rather than being asserted without backing
options.C: Claims never need support if they sound reasonable
options.D: Only the first claim in a document needs to be checked

questions.explanation: Each significant claim should be traceable to either in-document reasoning/evidence or an external source — unsupported assertions are a structural weakness.

questions.topic: Structural and Logical Consistency Evaluation
questions.question: A comparison document rates three vendors, but the written justification section only discusses two of them. What should a careful reviewer flag?

options.A: The document should be discarded and never reused
options.B: Nothing; this is a minor and acceptable oversight
options.C: The third vendor should be removed from consideration with no further explanation
options.D: The missing justification for the third vendor as an incompleteness/consistency gap that should be filled in before the document is used for a decision

questions.explanation: A gap between what's being compared and what's actually justified is a concrete completeness issue that should be caught and fixed.

questions.topic: Structural and Logical Consistency Evaluation
questions.question: Why is evaluating structure and logic considered a distinct skill from fact-checking specific claims?

options.A: Fact-checking is a subset of structural evaluation with no separate skill involved
options.B: Structure never matters if all facts are correct
options.C: A document can be built entirely from accurate individual facts and still have a flawed structure or an unsupported overall conclusion — each requires separate evaluation
options.D: They are the same skill and require no distinction

questions.explanation: Accuracy at the fact level doesn't guarantee soundness at the argument/structure level — both need to be checked independently.

questions.topic: Structural and Logical Consistency Evaluation
questions.question: A document's introduction promises to cover four topics, but the body only addresses three of them. What is the appropriate fix?

options.A: Either add the missing fourth topic to the body or revise the introduction to accurately reflect what the document actually covers
options.B: Add a note apologizing for the omission with no further correction
options.C: Delete the introduction entirely
options.D: Leave it as-is since three out of four is close enough

questions.explanation: Resolving the mismatch — by completing the content or correcting the promise — restores internal consistency between the introduction and the body.

questions.topic: SME Sign-Off Protocols for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: What does 'SME sign-off' mean in the context of reviewing AI-generated content?

options.A: Formal review and approval by a qualified Subject Matter Expert before high-stakes content (e.g., medical, legal, financial, safety) is finalized or acted upon
options.B: Automatic approval granted by the AI system itself
options.C: A step that is never necessary regardless of the content's stakes
options.D: A generic spell-check performed by any available employee

questions.explanation: SME sign-off is a human, qualified-expert review step specifically reserved for content where errors carry serious consequences.

questions.topic: SME Sign-Off Protocols for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: Claude drafts patient-facing guidance about medication dosages for a healthcare organization. What should happen before this content is distributed?

options.A: SME review is optional and can be skipped to save time
options.B: Only a grammar check is needed before distribution
options.C: It must be reviewed and formally approved by a qualified medical professional before distribution, given the safety stakes involved
options.D: It can be distributed immediately since it reads clearly and confidently

questions.explanation: Medical guidance affecting patient safety requires qualified expert sign-off regardless of how polished or confident the draft reads.

questions.topic: SME Sign-Off Protocols for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: Which category of content is most clearly identified as requiring SME sign-off before use?

options.A: An internal brainstorm list of possible team lunch spots
options.B: Medical, legal, financial, or safety-related guidance that could cause real harm if incorrect
options.C: A casual internal chat message with no external impact
options.D: A first-draft blog post idea with no publication plan

questions.explanation: High-stakes domains where errors cause real harm — medical, legal, financial, safety — are exactly where SME review is expected.

questions.topic: SME Sign-Off Protocols for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: An AI-drafted contract clause will be sent to an external counterparty. What is the appropriate process before sending?

options.A: Have a qualified legal reviewer examine and approve the clause before it is sent externally
options.B: Skip legal review since AI-generated text is inherently compliant
options.C: Send it directly since it reads as professionally worded
options.D: Only check the clause for spelling errors

questions.explanation: External contract language carries legal risk and requires qualified legal review before being sent, regardless of drafting quality.

questions.topic: SME Sign-Off Protocols for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: Why does polished, confident-sounding AI output NOT substitute for SME review in high-stakes domains?

options.A: Polished output is always accurate, so SME review is redundant
options.B: Fluency and confidence are stylistic properties that don't guarantee domain-specific correctness or compliance, which only a qualified expert can properly assess
options.C: SME review only matters for poorly written content
options.D: There is no meaningful difference between polish and correctness

questions.explanation: How something reads has no necessary connection to whether it's actually correct in a specialized, high-stakes domain — that requires genuine expertise to assess.

questions.topic: SME Sign-Off Protocols for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: A financial projection generated with AI assistance will be presented to investors. What is the appropriate sign-off process?

options.A: Present it directly since the calculations appear internally consistent
options.B: Have a qualified financial professional review the assumptions, methodology, and figures before the projection is presented externally
options.C: Skip review since investors will catch any errors themselves
options.D: Only check that the numbers are formatted with correct currency symbols

questions.explanation: Investor-facing financial projections carry real stakes and require qualified financial review of substance, not just formatting.

questions.topic: SME Sign-Off Protocols for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: What is a reasonable way to decide whether a given piece of AI-assisted content needs SME sign-off?

options.A: SME sign-off is never needed if the content was AI-generated, since AI is assumed reliable
options.B: Assess the potential consequences of an error — content where mistakes could cause real financial, legal, medical, or safety harm should get SME review
options.C: SME sign-off should be applied uniformly to every single piece of content regardless of stakes
options.D: Only content over a certain word count needs SME review

questions.explanation: Risk-based triage — based on the real-world consequences of an error — is the sound way to decide where SME review is warranted.

questions.topic: SME Sign-Off Protocols for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: An internal team uses Claude to draft a low-stakes internal FAQ about office supply ordering. Does this scenario require formal SME sign-off?

options.A: This scenario requires FDA approval
options.B: Yes, all AI-generated content requires the same level of formal expert sign-off
options.C: No review of any kind is ever appropriate for any AI-generated content
options.D: Not necessarily — light-touch internal review may be proportionate, since the consequences of an error here are low compared to medical, legal, financial, or safety content

questions.explanation: Sign-off rigor should scale with actual risk; a low-stakes internal FAQ doesn't carry the same consequences as regulated or safety-critical content.

questions.topic: SME Sign-Off Protocols for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: Who is qualified to provide SME sign-off on a piece of medical guidance content?

options.A: The AI model itself, since it generated the content
options.B: Whoever is available fastest, regardless of relevant expertise
options.C: Any employee who reads it and feels it sounds correct
options.D: A person with genuine, verifiable medical expertise relevant to the specific content being reviewed

questions.explanation: Sign-off requires genuine, relevant expertise — general confidence or availability doesn't substitute for actual qualification.

questions.topic: SME Sign-Off Protocols for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: A legal summary drafted with AI assistance will inform a significant business decision. Who should review it before the decision is finalized?

options.A: No one; the summary can be acted on directly
options.B: The original AI system, asked to confirm its own accuracy
options.C: A marketing team member with no legal background
options.D: A qualified legal professional, to confirm the summary's accuracy and completeness before it informs a significant decision

questions.explanation: A significant decision resting on legal accuracy warrants review by someone with actual legal qualification, not self-review by the AI.

questions.topic: SME Sign-Off Protocols for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: What is the risk of skipping SME sign-off on high-stakes content purely to save time?

options.A: There is no risk; time savings always outweigh review value
options.B: Skipping sign-off always improves the content's quality
options.C: An undetected error in a high-stakes domain (medical, legal, financial, safety) could cause real harm, liability, or costly consequences that far outweigh the time saved
options.D: SME review has no bearing on the actual accuracy of high-stakes content

questions.explanation: The potential cost of an undetected high-stakes error typically dwarfs the time saved by skipping expert review.

questions.topic: SME Sign-Off Protocols for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: A safety procedure document for handling equipment is drafted using Claude. What should happen before employees are trained on it?

options.A: Ask employees to identify errors themselves during training
options.B: Distribute it immediately since it appears complete and well-organized
options.C: Skip expert review since safety documents are self-explanatory
options.D: Have it reviewed and approved by a qualified safety expert familiar with the actual equipment and procedures before it's used for training

questions.explanation: Safety procedures directly affect physical wellbeing and require qualified expert validation before being used operationally.

questions.topic: SME Sign-Off Protocols for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: Why is it important to identify high-stakes content categories (medical, legal, financial, safety) as a standard part of a review workflow?

options.A: It isn't important; all content should be treated identically
options.B: Explicitly flagging these categories ensures the appropriate level of expert review is consistently triggered, rather than relying on ad hoc judgment calls
options.C: This categorization only matters for very large organizations
options.D: High-stakes categories never actually appear in typical business use of Claude

questions.explanation: A consistent, explicit categorization process ensures higher-risk content reliably gets the review it needs, rather than depending on inconsistent individual judgment.

questions.topic: SME Sign-Off Protocols for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: An AI-assisted risk assessment for a construction project needs to go to stakeholders. What is the appropriate process?

options.A: Publish it publicly before any internal review
options.B: Send it directly with no additional review
options.C: Have the marketing team review it for tone only
options.D: Route it through a qualified engineering or safety professional for review and approval given the safety and liability stakes

questions.explanation: Construction safety and liability stakes call for qualified engineering/safety expert review before stakeholder distribution.

questions.topic: SME Sign-Off Protocols for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: What should a business's AI usage policy typically specify regarding high-stakes content?

options.A: No guidance is necessary since employees will figure it out individually
options.B: That high-stakes content should never be drafted with AI assistance under any circumstances
options.C: That AI-generated high-stakes content can always be used without any human review
options.D: Clear criteria for which content categories require mandatory SME review before use, and by whom

questions.explanation: Clear, explicit policy criteria for mandatory review help ensure consistent, appropriate handling of high-stakes content across an organization.

questions.topic: SME Sign-Off Protocols for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: A user is unsure whether a piece of content is 'high-stakes enough' to require SME sign-off. What is a reasonable default?

options.A: Always assume no review is needed to save time
options.B: Flip a coin to decide
options.C: When in doubt, especially for medical, legal, financial, or safety-adjacent content, err toward seeking expert review rather than skipping it
options.D: Assume it never needs review unless told otherwise explicitly

questions.explanation: Given the asymmetric cost of an undetected high-stakes error, erring toward review in ambiguous cases is the safer default.

questions.topic: SME Sign-Off Protocols for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: Which best describes the relationship between AI assistance and professional accountability in high-stakes domains?

options.A: AI assistance fully replaces the need for professional accountability
options.B: There is no relationship between the two concepts
options.C: Professional accountability disappears once AI is involved in drafting
options.D: AI can accelerate drafting, but a qualified professional remains accountable for verifying and approving high-stakes content before it's relied upon

questions.explanation: AI assistance changes how a draft is produced, not who is ultimately accountable for its accuracy and appropriateness in high-stakes domains.

questions.topic: Choosing Output Format (Artifacts vs Inline vs Structured Data)
questions.question: When is it most appropriate to render a response as a standalone visual artifact (e.g., a diagram or interactive component) rather than inline text?

options.A: When the content is substantial, reusable, or benefits from a visual/interactive form (e.g., a chart, a reusable document, a diagram) rather than a quick conversational answer
options.B: Always, regardless of the content's nature
options.C: Only when the user explicitly types the word 'artifact'
options.D: Never; all content should remain inline

questions.explanation: Artifacts earn their place for standalone, reusable, or visually/structurally rich content — not for quick conversational answers.

questions.topic: Choosing Output Format (Artifacts vs Inline vs Structured Data)
questions.question: A user asks a quick clarifying question expecting a one-sentence answer. Should this be rendered as a standalone artifact?

options.A: Yes, all responses should default to being artifacts
options.B: No — a quick, short, conversational answer is better kept inline rather than turned into a separate document-like artifact
options.C: Only if the answer contains any numbers
options.D: Only if the user is using a mobile device

questions.explanation: Brief conversational answers don't benefit from being pulled out into a separate artifact — that adds friction rather than value.

questions.topic: Choosing Output Format (Artifacts vs Inline vs Structured Data)
questions.question: Which output format is generally most appropriate for data meant to be imported directly into a spreadsheet?

options.A: A poem summarizing the data
options.B: A long narrative paragraph with numbers embedded in prose
options.C: Structured, tabular data (e.g., a clean table or CSV-style format) that can be pasted directly into rows and columns
options.D: An image of the data with no underlying structure

questions.explanation: Structured, tabular output is directly usable in a spreadsheet, unlike prose or non-structured formats.

questions.topic: Choosing Output Format (Artifacts vs Inline vs Structured Data)
questions.question: A user needs a diagram showing a multi-step approval process for a presentation. Which output format best serves this need?

options.A: A single word answer
options.B: A dense paragraph describing each step in prose
options.C: An unformatted block of text with no structure
options.D: A visual diagram/flowchart artifact that can be viewed and potentially reused directly

questions.explanation: A visual process is best served by an actual diagram rather than prose description, especially when it will be reused in a presentation.

questions.topic: Choosing Output Format (Artifacts vs Inline vs Structured Data)
questions.question: What is a downside of rendering every response — even simple, short ones — as a separate artifact?

options.A: Artifacts always take longer to generate with no other tradeoff
options.B: Artifacts cannot contain any text at all
options.C: It can add unnecessary friction and clutter for content that would be perfectly usable as a normal conversational reply
options.D: There is no downside; more artifacts are always better

questions.explanation: Over-using artifacts for simple content adds friction without adding value — the format should match the content's actual needs.

questions.topic: Choosing Output Format (Artifacts vs Inline vs Structured Data)
questions.question: A user wants a document they can keep editing and referring back to over several sessions, such as a living project plan. Which format is most appropriate?

options.A: An inline conversational answer that isn't saved as a distinct, reusable document
options.B: A single emoji
options.C: A standalone artifact/document format that persists and can be revisited and edited over time
options.D: A verbal-only description with no written form at all

questions.explanation: Content meant to be revisited and edited over time is better served by a persistent, standalone document than a one-off inline reply.

questions.topic: Choosing Output Format (Artifacts vs Inline vs Structured Data)
questions.question: Which factor should most influence the choice between inline text and a structured table for presenting comparison data?

options.A: The user's personal favorite color
options.B: The time of day the request was made
options.C: Whether the request included any punctuation
options.D: Whether the data has multiple comparable dimensions (e.g., comparing several options across several criteria) that a table would make clearer than prose

questions.explanation: Multi-dimensional comparisons are typically much clearer in tabular form than buried in prose.

questions.topic: Choosing Output Format (Artifacts vs Inline vs Structured Data)
questions.question: A user asks for '3 quick pros and cons' of a decision in the middle of an ongoing chat conversation. What is the most proportionate output format?

options.A: An interactive data visualization
options.B: A single-word response with no list at all
options.C: A full standalone document artifact with a title page
options.D: A brief inline list directly in the conversation, matching the quick, conversational nature of the request

questions.explanation: A quick, small list embedded in an ongoing conversation is well-served by a simple inline reply, not a heavyweight standalone artifact.

questions.topic: Choosing Output Format (Artifacts vs Inline vs Structured Data)
questions.question: Why might structured data (e.g., a table or list with consistent fields) be preferable to free-form prose for information that will be processed further (e.g., imported into another tool)?

options.A: Structured, consistent fields are far easier to parse, sort, filter, or import into another system than unstructured prose
options.B: There is no difference in downstream usability between the two formats
options.C: Structured data can never include any actual information
options.D: Prose is always easier for downstream tools to process

questions.explanation: Downstream tools generally need consistent, structured fields to process data reliably — prose requires manual extraction first.

questions.topic: Choosing Output Format (Artifacts vs Inline vs Structured Data)
questions.question: A user requests 'a simple explanation of this concept' in a casual chat. Which format best matches this request?

options.A: A concise inline explanation appropriate to a casual conversational exchange
options.B: A complex interactive simulation
options.C: A multi-page standalone document with a table of contents
options.D: A spreadsheet with no explanatory text at all

questions.explanation: Matching format weight to the request's actual scope avoids over-engineering a simple conversational ask.

questions.topic: Choosing Output Format (Artifacts vs Inline vs Structured Data)
questions.question: What is a reasonable guideline for deciding when content should be a reusable artifact rather than a one-off inline reply?

options.A: Every response, regardless of content, should be an artifact
options.B: Format choice should be entirely random
options.C: If the content is substantial, likely to be reused/edited/shared as a standalone piece, or benefits from a visual/structured presentation, an artifact is likely appropriate
options.D: No response should ever be an artifact

questions.explanation: The key signals are substance, reusability, and whether visual/structural presentation adds real value — not an arbitrary default in either direction.

questions.topic: Choosing Output Format (Artifacts vs Inline vs Structured Data)
questions.question: A user needs both a short conversational answer AND a separate, polished document version of the same content for distribution. What is a reasonable approach?

options.A: Only ever provide one or the other, never both
options.B: Provide the quick conversational answer inline, and separately produce a polished, standalone artifact version suited for distribution
options.C: Combine both into a single confusing response with no clear distinction
options.D: Refuse the request since it has two parts

questions.explanation: Serving each need with the format suited to it — quick inline answer plus a separate polished artifact — satisfies both without compromising either.

questions.topic: Choosing Output Format (Artifacts vs Inline vs Structured Data)
questions.question: Why does matching output format to actual downstream use matter for business productivity?

options.A: Format only matters for aesthetic reasons with no productivity impact
options.B: Business users never care about output format
options.C: Content in the wrong format (e.g., prose where a table was needed) often requires manual rework, costing time that correct format selection would have avoided
options.D: It doesn't matter; format never affects how usable content is

questions.explanation: Mismatched format creates avoidable rework — correct format selection is a genuine productivity consideration, not just an aesthetic preference.

questions.topic: Verifying Numerical and Statistical Claims
questions.question: Why do numerical and statistical claims deserve particular scrutiny in AI-generated business content?

options.A: Numbers carry an appearance of precision and objectivity that can mask an underlying error or fabrication, and are easy to state confidently even when wrong
options.B: Statistical claims are never used in business writing
options.C: Numbers are always self-evidently correct and need no scrutiny
options.D: Numbers are the only type of content ever worth checking

questions.explanation: The apparent precision of a number can create false confidence, making numerical claims a particularly important category to verify.

questions.question: A report states 'sales grew by 34%' with no baseline period specified. What is the issue?

options.A: The number should simply be doubled to correct it
options.B: Percentages never require a stated baseline
options.C: Without knowing the comparison baseline (e.g., year-over-year vs. month-over-month, and which specific periods), the percentage is ambiguous and potentially misleading
options.D: There is no issue; the percentage alone is sufficient information

questions.explanation: A percentage without a clear, specific baseline period is ambiguous and can be interpreted (or misused) in misleading ways.

questions.topic: Verifying Numerical and Statistical Claims
questions.question: What should a careful reviewer check when a statistic is presented as an average?

options.A: Nothing further; averages are always representative
options.B: Whether the number is even or odd
options.C: Whether the average might be skewed by outliers, and whether a median or another measure would better represent the actual data
options.D: The color used to display the number

questions.explanation: Averages can be distorted by outliers, so understanding what's driving the number is part of responsibly verifying and presenting it.

questions.topic: Verifying Numerical and Statistical Claims
questions.question: A claim states '9 out of 10 customers prefer our product' based on a survey. What follow-up question is most important before using this claim publicly?

options.A: No follow-up is needed; the ratio alone is sufficient
options.B: What font was used in the survey report?
options.C: What time of day was the survey conducted?
options.D: What was the actual sample size, and is it large and representative enough to support this claim confidently?

questions.explanation: Sample size and representativeness are essential context for whether a ratio-based claim is actually meaningful and defensible.

questions.topic: Verifying Numerical and Statistical Claims
questions.question: Why might a very precise-looking number (e.g., '73.6% improvement') actually warrant more scrutiny, not less?

options.A: Precision has no bearing on whether scrutiny is warranted
options.B: Precise numbers are always safe to use without checking
options.C: Excessive false precision can be a sign of a fabricated or miscalculated figure, since real-world business data is often messier or rounder than that
options.D: Precision always indicates rigorous measurement and should never be questioned

questions.explanation: Oddly precise figures in contexts where such precision wouldn't realistically exist can be a subtle sign of fabrication.

questions.topic: Verifying Numerical and Statistical Claims
questions.question: Two different sections of the same report state different total figures for what should be the same metric. What should a careful reviewer do?

options.A: Ignore the discrepancy since both numbers are probably close enough
options.B: Delete both numbers and leave the metric blank with no explanation
options.C: Average the two numbers together with no further investigation
options.D: Investigate and reconcile the discrepancy before finalizing the report, since inconsistent figures for the same metric undermine the report's credibility

questions.explanation: Inconsistent figures for the same metric within one document is a credibility-damaging error that needs to be resolved, not glossed over.

questions.topic: Verifying Numerical and Statistical Claims
questions.question: What is a reasonable check when a statistic is used to support a strong claim (e.g., 'this proves X is always true')?

options.A: Verify whether the underlying data actually supports a claim that strong, since a single statistic often supports a more limited or qualified conclusion than an absolute claim implies
options.B: Replace the statistic with a stronger-sounding one
options.C: Strong claims never need statistical support
options.D: Assume any statistic automatically justifies any strength of claim

questions.explanation: Statistical evidence often supports more limited, qualified conclusions than sweeping absolute claims — checking this alignment is part of responsible use.

questions.topic: Verifying Numerical and Statistical Claims
questions.question: A projection extrapolates a trend from only two data points. What should a careful reviewer flag?

options.A: Nothing; two data points are always sufficient for a reliable trend
options.B: The limited reliability of a trend based on so little data, and whether more data points are needed before treating the projection as dependable
options.C: The font size of the projection chart
options.D: The specific day of the week the data was collected

questions.explanation: Extrapolating confidently from very few data points is a real statistical weakness worth flagging before the projection is relied upon.

questions.topic: Verifying Numerical and Statistical Claims
questions.question: Why is it important to check whether a percentage change is expressed correctly (e.g., percentage points vs. relative percentage)?

options.A: The distinction never matters in practice
options.B: Percentage points and relative percentages always mean exactly the same thing
options.C: This distinction is only relevant in academic statistics, never in business
options.D: Confusing percentage points with relative percentage change can produce a claim that is technically misleading, even if no individual number is 'made up'

questions.explanation: Percentage-point vs. relative-percentage confusion is a real, common way to produce a misleading claim without any individual fabricated number.

questions.topic: Verifying Numerical and Statistical Claims
questions.question: A dashboard summary claims a metric 'doubled' based on a comparison between two very small numbers (e.g., 2 to 4). What context is important to include?

options.A: The small absolute numbers involved, since 'doubled' from a tiny base can create a misleadingly dramatic impression compared to the actual magnitude of change
options.B: Only the percentage matters; absolute numbers are irrelevant
options.C: The claim should be changed to 'tripled' instead
options.D: No context is needed; 'doubled' is a complete and sufficient claim on its own

questions.explanation: Relative framing ('doubled') without absolute context can create a misleading impression of significance when the underlying numbers are actually small.

questions.topic: Verifying Numerical and Statistical Claims
questions.question: What is a sound general habit for handling any statistic before it's used in a significant business decision?

options.A: Ask where it came from, what it's actually measuring, and whether the underlying methodology supports the way it's being used
options.B: Only check statistics that appear in the introduction of a document
options.C: Use the number as presented with no further questions
options.D: Assume larger numbers are always more trustworthy than smaller ones

questions.explanation: Understanding provenance, definition, and methodology is the core discipline behind responsibly using any statistic in a real decision.

questions.topic: Verifying Numerical and Statistical Claims
questions.question: A response states a specific correlation between two business metrics and implies one causes the other. What should a careful reader question?

options.B: The claim should be accepted since it involves numbers
options.C: Only the units used for each metric need checking
options.D: Whether the evidence actually supports a causal claim, or only shows the two metrics moving together without establishing that one causes the other

questions.explanation: Correlation-implies-causation is a classic reasoning gap worth checking whenever a causal claim is made from what may only be a correlational observation.

questions.topic: Recognizing Confidently-Wrong Answers (Overconfidence Cues)

questions.topic: Recognizing Confidently-Wrong Answers (Overconfidence Cues)

options.B: Whichever response is longer is automatically more accurate

questions.topic: Recognizing Confidently-Wrong Answers (Overconfidence Cues)

options.C: Shorter responses are always more accurate than longer ones
options.D: Length and detail are the only reliable accuracy signals available

questions.topic: Recognizing Confidently-Wrong Answers (Overconfidence Cues)

questions.topic: Recognizing Confidently-Wrong Answers (Overconfidence Cues)
questions.question: What role does independent verification play in counteracting the risk of confidently-wrong answers?

options.A: Verification is only useful for catching hedged, uncertain answers
options.B: Verification should only be applied to responses that sound uncertain
options.C: It's the concrete corrective step — since tone and style aren't reliable accuracy signals, an external, independent check is what actually confirms correctness
options.D: No role; independent verification cannot help with this issue

questions.explanation: Because internal cues like tone are unreliable, an external verification step is the substantive corrective — regardless of how confident or hedged the original response sounded.

questions.topic: Recognizing Confidently-Wrong Answers (Overconfidence Cues)
questions.question: A user is evaluating whether to trust a business recommendation from Claude. Which approach best reflects sound evaluation practice?

questions.question: You're designing a workflow where Claude assists with issuing customer refunds. Which design reflects a sound human-in-the-loop checkpoint?
