options.A: This consideration only applies to non-business Projects
options.B: Live, frequently-updating documents should never be used as knowledge sources under any circumstances
options.C: No consideration is needed; the knowledge source will always automatically reflect the very latest live version with no user action
options.D: Understanding how and when the uploaded reference material needs to be refreshed to stay reasonably current, since a one-time upload reflects only a snapshot

questions.explanation: A knowledge source added as an upload is a snapshot at that point in time — understanding the need to refresh it is important for a frequently-changing source.

questions.topic: Knowledge Source Configuration
questions.question: What is a reasonable principle for scoping which documents belong in a given Project's knowledge sources?

options.A: Include as many documents as possible from across the entire organization regardless of relevance
options.B: Include no documents at all under any circumstances
options.C: Scoping should be based purely on document file size
options.D: Include documents that are genuinely relevant to that Project's specific purpose, keeping the knowledge base focused rather than diluted with unrelated material

questions.explanation: Relevance to the Project's actual purpose — not sheer volume or file size — is the sound basis for scoping knowledge sources.

questions.topic: Knowledge Source Configuration
questions.question: A user adds a knowledge source containing outdated contact information for a partner organization. Later, responses reference this outdated contact. What is the root cause and fix?

options.A: The outdated knowledge source is the root cause; updating or removing it is the direct fix to prevent further outdated references
options.B: This is not fixable under any circumstances
options.C: The issue can only be fixed by deleting the entire Project
options.D: The root cause is unrelated to the knowledge source; no fix related to it is needed

questions.explanation: Tracing the outdated reference back to its source material and updating or removing that source is the direct, appropriate fix.

questions.topic: Knowledge Source Configuration
questions.question: Why is scoping knowledge sources tightly to a Project's purpose generally preferable to adding broad, loosely-related material 'just in case'?

options.A: Broad, loosely-related material always improves response quality with no downside
options.B: Scoping considerations are irrelevant to response quality
options.C: 'Just in case' inclusion is always the best default strategy
options.D: Tightly-scoped, relevant sources reduce the risk of irrelevant or contradictory material diluting or confusing responses, and reduce unnecessary exposure of unrelated content

questions.explanation: Focused knowledge sources reduce dilution/contradiction risk and avoid unnecessarily exposing unrelated content within that Project's context.

questions.topic: Custom Instructions Scope and Precedence
questions.question: A user wants a one-time exception to a Project's standing formatting rule for a single specific request. What is the appropriate way to express this?

options.A: Permanently delete the Project's standing formatting rule to accommodate the one-time exception
options.B: Explicitly state the desired exception for that specific request, understanding it applies to this instance without needing to change the underlying standing rule
options.C: Assume exceptions are never possible and abandon the request
options.D: Create an entirely new Project just for this one exception

questions.explanation: A clearly stated, request-specific exception is the proportionate way to handle a one-off deviation without altering the standing default.

questions.topic: Custom Instructions Scope and Precedence
questions.question: What is a reasonable way to think about the relationship between a Project's standing instructions and a specific in-conversation request?

options.A: The standing instructions and specific requests can never coexist or interact in any way
options.B: Specific requests are always completely ignored in favor of standing instructions with no exception
options.C: The standing instructions provide a consistent default, while a specific request can reasonably adjust behavior for that instance, similar to how a general policy can allow for specific, stated exceptions
options.D: Standing instructions are always completely ignored in favor of the most recent specific request

questions.explanation: This relationship mirrors general-policy-with-specific-exception reasoning: a sensible default that can flex for an explicitly stated, specific case.

questions.topic: Custom Instructions Scope and Precedence
questions.question: A user is troubleshooting why a Project seems to apply a rule inconsistently across different conversations. What is a good diagnostic step?

options.A: Assume the inconsistency is unexplainable and cannot be investigated
options.B: Assume all conversations within a Project always behave identically regardless of configuration
options.C: Check whether the rule was actually set at the Project level (applying to all conversations) versus having only been mentioned in one specific past conversation
options.D: Delete the Project immediately with no further diagnosis

questions.explanation: Confirming the actual scope where a rule was set (Project-wide vs. one conversation) is the direct way to diagnose apparent inconsistency.

questions.topic: Custom Instructions Scope and Precedence
questions.question: Why is it useful to think of Project-level instructions as 'defaults' rather than absolute, unchangeable rules?

options.A: Defaults and absolute rules are identical concepts with no meaningful difference
options.B: This framing implies Project instructions have no effect at all
options.C: Thinking of them as defaults captures how they provide consistent baseline behavior while still reasonably accommodating specific, explicitly stated exceptions for individual requests
options.D: This framing is inaccurate and should never be used

questions.explanation: The 'default' framing captures the practical reality: consistent baseline behavior that can still flex for a clearly stated specific case.

questions.topic: Custom Instructions Scope and Precedence
questions.question: A user wants to permanently change a Project's standing behavior, not just make a one-time exception. What is the appropriate action?

options.A: Update the actual Project-level custom instructions, since that is the mechanism for changing standing, persistent behavior going forward
options.B: Create a brand new, entirely separate account to achieve this change
options.C: State the change only within a single conversation and expect it to permanently alter the Project's standing configuration
options.D: Permanent changes to standing behavior are not possible under any circumstances

questions.explanation: A genuinely permanent change to standing behavior requires updating the Project-level instructions themselves, not just a one-off in-conversation statement.

questions.topic: Organizing Projects for Teams
questions.question: A team has grown from a single small group into several distinct sub-teams with different clients. What organizational adjustment is likely warranted?

options.A: Continue using exactly one shared Project for all sub-teams and all clients indefinitely with no changes
options.B: Merge every sub-team's work into a single conversation with no Project structure at all
options.C: Consider splitting into separate Projects aligned with each sub-team/client's distinct context, instructions, and knowledge sources
options.D: Eliminate all Projects and revert to entirely unconfigured conversations

questions.explanation: As distinct contexts emerge across sub-teams/clients, splitting into appropriately scoped separate Projects better serves each group's specific needs.

questions.topic: Organizing Projects for Teams
questions.question: What is a risk of having too many overlapping, redundant Projects covering nearly the same work?

options.A: Redundant Projects can lead to inconsistent configuration (different instructions/knowledge sources for what should be the same context) and confusion about which Project to use
options.B: This scenario is not possible to create
options.C: There is no risk; more Projects are always better regardless of overlap
options.D: Overlapping Projects always automatically merge with no issue

questions.explanation: Redundant, overlapping Projects risk inconsistent configuration and confusion about where a given piece of work should actually happen.

questions.topic: Organizing Projects for Teams
questions.question: A newly formed cross-functional team needs a shared space with consistent context for a specific initiative involving multiple departments. What is a reasonable setup?

options.A: Have each department maintain entirely separate, disconnected configurations with no shared context
options.B: Set up a single shared Project for the initiative, configured with the context and knowledge sources relevant to the cross-functional work
options.C: Avoid setting up any shared configuration since the team is cross-functional
options.D: Require each individual to memorize the initiative's context with no configured support

questions.explanation: A single shared Project tailored to the initiative gives the cross-functional team the consistent context it needs.

questions.topic: Organizing Projects for Teams
questions.question: Why might assigning clear ownership for maintaining a shared team Project's configuration be a good practice?

options.A: Ownership is irrelevant; shared Projects maintain themselves automatically
options.B: Assigning ownership always makes shared Projects worse
options.C: Only individual, non-shared Projects can have an owner
options.D: Without clear ownership, a shared Project's instructions and knowledge sources may drift out of date with no one responsible for keeping them current

questions.explanation: Clear ownership ensures someone is actually responsible for keeping a shared Project's configuration accurate and current over time.

questions.topic: Data Privacy and Sensitive Information Handling
questions.question: A user needs Claude's help drafting a document that references a real, specific dollar amount from an unreleased financial figure. What is a privacy-conscious approach if the exact figure isn't essential for the drafting task?

options.A: Always include the exact real figure regardless of necessity
options.B: Consider using a placeholder or rounded illustrative figure for drafting purposes if the exact real number isn't actually needed to complete the task
options.C: Refuse to draft any document that could ever involve financial figures
options.D: Share as many additional unreleased figures as possible for context

questions.explanation: Using a placeholder when the exact sensitive figure isn't actually necessary for the task is a practical data-minimization step.

questions.topic: Data Privacy and Sensitive Information Handling
questions.question: What is a reasonable relationship between data sensitivity and the level of caution applied before sharing it in any tool, including Claude?

options.A: More sensitive data (financial, health, personal identifiers, confidential business information) warrants proportionally more caution and scrutiny of applicable policy before sharing
options.B: Caution should decrease as sensitivity increases
options.C: Sensitivity has no bearing on how data should be handled
options.D: All data should be treated with identical caution regardless of sensitivity

questions.explanation: Proportional caution — more scrutiny for more sensitive categories — is the sound, risk-based approach to data handling.

questions.topic: Data Privacy and Sensitive Information Handling
questions.question: An employee is unsure whether a specific internal document counts as 'confidential' under their organization's policy. What is the appropriate action?

options.A: Check the organization's classification policy or ask an appropriate contact to confirm the document's sensitivity level before sharing it
options.B: Assume all documents are always confidential and never use Claude for any related work
options.C: Assume it is not confidential and share it freely with no verification
options.D: Make a private guess with no reference to any organizational standard

questions.explanation: Verifying against the actual organizational classification (or asking) is more reliable than assuming or guessing about a document's sensitivity.

questions.topic: Data Privacy and Sensitive Information Handling
questions.question: Why might anonymizing or redacting identifying details be a reasonable practice when the specific identity isn't necessary for a task?

options.A: Anonymizing details is never useful for any task involving sensitive data
options.B: This practice is only relevant to government organizations
options.C: Anonymizing details always makes tasks impossible to complete
options.D: It reduces exposure of unnecessary personal or confidential information while still allowing the underlying task to be completed effectively

questions.explanation: Removing unnecessary identifying detail is a practical way to reduce exposure while still getting the actual task done.

questions.topic: Data Privacy and Sensitive Information Handling
questions.question: A user is drafting internal training material and wants to use a realistic example involving customer data. What is a privacy-conscious approach?

options.A: Use a fictional or clearly anonymized example that illustrates the same point without exposing real customer information
options.B: Use real customer data but only share it with a few colleagues
options.C: Use real, actual customer data taken directly from live records
options.D: Avoid creating any training materials that involve examples

questions.explanation: A fictional or anonymized example serves the training purpose just as well without exposing actual customer data.

questions.topic: Data Privacy and Sensitive Information Handling
questions.question: What is a reasonable default when a task could be completed either with real sensitive data or an anonymized/synthetic equivalent?

options.A: Always default to using the real sensitive data for maximum realism regardless of necessity
options.B: Prefer the anonymized/synthetic equivalent when it serves the task's actual purpose just as well, minimizing unnecessary exposure of real sensitive data
options.C: The choice between the two options never matters from a privacy perspective
options.D: Synthetic data should never be used under any circumstances

questions.explanation: Preferring anonymized/synthetic data when it serves the purpose equally well is a sound, low-cost privacy practice.

questions.topic: Responsible AI Use Principles
questions.question: A team uses Claude to draft public-facing statements about a sensitive company event. What responsible-use consideration is most relevant?

options.A: No consideration is needed since drafting is just a starting point
options.B: Careful human review for accuracy, tone, and appropriateness before any public-facing statement is released, given the reputational and factual stakes involved
options.C: Public statements should always be sent exactly as first drafted
options.D: This scenario has no meaningful responsible-use considerations

questions.explanation: Public-facing, reputationally significant statements warrant careful human review before release, regardless of how the draft was produced.

questions.topic: Responsible AI Use Principles
questions.question: Why is 'verify before relying on' a central theme across many responsible AI use principles?

options.A: Because AI-generated content can be fluent yet inaccurate or inappropriate, verification is the practical safeguard that lets people benefit from AI assistance while managing its risks
options.B: Verification is never actually necessary in practice
options.C: Verification only matters for creative writing tasks
options.D: This theme applies only to technical, coding-related use cases

questions.explanation: Verification is the practical bridge between AI's genuine usefulness and the real risk that fluent output can still be wrong or inappropriate.

questions.topic: Responsible AI Use Principles
questions.question: An employee wants to use Claude to help draft feedback for a colleague's performance review. What is a responsible approach?

options.A: Send the AI-drafted feedback directly with no personal review or judgment applied
options.B: Avoid providing any personal input to feedback under any circumstances
options.C: Use the draft as a starting point, then apply personal judgment and direct knowledge of the colleague's actual performance before finalizing the feedback
options.D: Responsible use principles don't apply to performance feedback

questions.explanation: Personal judgment and direct knowledge should still shape and validate AI-assisted feedback before it's finalized, given its impact on a real person.

questions.topic: Responsible AI Use Principles
questions.question: What is a reasonable way to think about the balance between efficiency gains from AI assistance and responsible use?

options.A: Efficiency should always be sacrificed entirely in favor of responsible use, with no middle ground
options.B: Efficiency and responsible use are always in complete conflict with no way to balance them
options.C: Responsible use principles should always be abandoned in favor of maximum efficiency
options.D: AI assistance can provide real efficiency gains while responsible practices (verification, appropriate review, privacy awareness) manage the accompanying risks — the two can coexist with thoughtful workflow design

questions.explanation: Thoughtful workflow design lets efficiency gains and responsible-use safeguards coexist, rather than treating them as strictly opposed.

questions.topic: Responsible AI Use Principles
questions.question: A user is drafting content that will influence a decision about resource allocation between departments. What responsible-use consideration applies?

options.A: Given the potential for this content to meaningfully influence a consequential internal decision, applying appropriate scrutiny and verification before it's used is warranted
options.B: Only content shared externally ever requires responsible-use consideration
options.C: None; resource-allocation content requires no particular care
options.D: This type of content should never involve any AI assistance

questions.explanation: Content that meaningfully influences a consequential decision — even an internal one — warrants proportional scrutiny before being relied upon.

questions.topic: Recognizing When Human Review or Escalation Is Required
questions.question: While drafting a response to a customer, a user notices language suggesting the customer may be in personal crisis. What is the appropriate action?

options.A: Escalate to the appropriate internal process or trained personnel for handling sensitive personal situations, rather than treating it as a routine drafting task
options.B: Have Claude draft a purely transactional response and send it with no further consideration
options.C: Ignore the concerning language entirely since it's outside the scope of the original request
options.D: Ask Claude to resolve the personal crisis directly with no human involvement

questions.explanation: Signs of a potential personal crisis call for escalation to appropriate trained personnel or processes, not a purely transactional AI-drafted response.

questions.topic: Recognizing When Human Review or Escalation Is Required
questions.question: Why might repeated, unexplained errors in an AI-assisted process be a signal for escalation beyond just fixing the immediate error?

options.A: Repeated errors are never worth escalating beyond the immediate fix
options.B: A persistent pattern of errors may indicate a deeper issue with how the process or tool is being used, which is worth surfacing to someone who can address the root cause
options.C: Repeated errors should always be resolved by simply ignoring them
options.D: This pattern has no bearing on whether escalation is warranted

questions.explanation: A persistent error pattern is a signal worth escalating beyond a one-off fix, since it may point to a systemic issue needing broader attention.

questions.topic: Recognizing When Human Review or Escalation Is Required
questions.question: A user is asked to use Claude to help with a task that seems to conflict with a stated organizational value or policy. What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Raise the apparent conflict with an appropriate person (e.g., a manager or compliance contact) before proceeding, rather than resolving the tension unilaterally
options.B: Refuse all future work indefinitely without raising the specific concern to anyone
options.C: Assume the conflict doesn't matter since AI is involved
options.D: Proceed with the task regardless of the apparent conflict

questions.explanation: Surfacing an apparent policy conflict to the appropriate person — rather than resolving it unilaterally or ignoring it — is the responsible escalation path.

questions.topic: Recognizing When Human Review or Escalation Is Required
questions.question: What is a reasonable way to build organizational awareness of when escalation is appropriate for AI-assisted work?

options.A: Assume all employees will intuitively know when to escalate with no guidance provided
options.B: Provide clear examples and criteria (e.g., legal, safety, compliance, or significant consequence scenarios) as part of training and policy, so escalation triggers are well understood
options.C: Escalation criteria should be kept intentionally vague to avoid over-escalation
options.D: Escalation guidance is unnecessary since AI-assisted work never requires it

questions.explanation: Concrete examples and clear criteria in training/policy help build shared, consistent understanding of when escalation is actually warranted.

questions.topic: Risk Categorization for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: A document will be used only for internal brainstorming with no external distribution and no decision directly resting on it. How should this generally be categorized?

options.A: Medium-high risk regardless of audience or actual use
options.B: Risk category cannot be assessed for brainstorming documents under any circumstances
options.C: High risk, equivalent to an external regulatory filing
options.D: Generally lower risk, given the limited audience and lack of direct consequential decision resting on it — though this can change if its use later expands

questions.explanation: Limited audience and lack of direct consequential reliance are exactly the factors that generally place content in a lower risk category — though that categorization should be revisited if its use expands.

questions.topic: Risk Categorization for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: Why is risk categorization better understood as an ongoing assessment rather than a one-time label applied at creation?

options.A: The same content's actual risk can change as its intended use, audience, or distribution changes over time, so re-assessment may be warranted
options.B: Risk categorization should always be a permanent, one-time label with no reconsideration
options.C: Only the original creator's assessment ever matters, regardless of how the content is later used
options.D: Risk categorization is entirely arbitrary and provides no ongoing value

questions.explanation: Because actual risk depends on evolving use and audience, treating categorization as an ongoing check (not a permanent one-time label) is more accurate.

questions.topic: Risk Categorization for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: A piece of content was originally created for internal use (low risk) but is now being considered for external publication. What should happen?

options.A: Re-assess the content's risk category in light of the new external audience and apply the level of review appropriate to that higher-stakes context before publishing
options.B: External publication requires no additional scrutiny beyond the original internal review
options.C: Publish it externally with no reassessment, since it was already reviewed once for internal use
options.D: Risk category never needs to be reconsidered once content has been created

questions.explanation: A meaningful change in audience/use (internal to external) warrants re-categorizing risk and applying appropriately elevated review before publication.

questions.topic: Risk Categorization for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: What is a reasonable way to handle content that is genuinely ambiguous between two risk categories (e.g., between low and medium risk)?

options.A: Always default to treating ambiguous content as the lowest possible risk to save time
options.B: When genuinely ambiguous, erring toward the higher of the two plausible categories is a reasonably safe default, applying somewhat more review than might strictly be necessary
options.C: Ambiguous content should never be assessed at all
options.D: Ambiguity should be resolved by flipping a coin with no further judgment

questions.explanation: Given the asymmetric cost of under-reviewing higher-stakes content, erring toward the higher plausible category is a reasonably safe default in genuinely ambiguous cases.

questions.topic: Organizational Policy Compliance for AI Use
questions.question: An employee working across two different client accounts wonders if the same AI usage rules apply identically to both. What is a reasonable check?

options.A: Ignore client-specific considerations entirely
options.B: Assume no organizational policy could ever vary by client
options.C: Check whether either client relationship carries specific contractual or regulatory requirements that might mean different rules apply for each account
options.D: Assume identical rules apply to all clients with no verification

questions.explanation: Client-specific contractual or regulatory requirements can mean different rules genuinely apply per account, making a specific check worthwhile.

questions.topic: Organizational Policy Compliance for AI Use
questions.question: Why might an organization's AI policy explicitly list prohibited use cases in addition to approved ones?

options.A: Only approved-use lists are ever useful; prohibited-use lists are redundant
options.B: Prohibited-use lists serve no practical purpose
options.C: Prohibited-use lists are only relevant to non-AI tools
options.D: Explicitly naming known problematic use cases (e.g., certain high-risk or regulated activities) provides clear guardrails alongside the guidance on approved uses

questions.explanation: Explicit prohibited-use guidance provides clear guardrails for known problem areas, complementing guidance on what's approved.

questions.topic: Output Truncation and Token Limits
questions.question: A user repeatedly hits truncation on the same type of large recurring request. What is a more durable fix than repeatedly asking to 'continue' each time?

options.A: Restructure the recurring request into smaller, planned sections from the outset, so truncation is avoided proactively rather than fixed reactively each time
options.B: Continue tolerating repeated manual 'continue' requests indefinitely with no process change
options.C: Randomly change the topic of the request each time
options.D: Stop making this type of request altogether

questions.explanation: Proactively restructuring a recurring large request into planned sections is a more durable fix than repeatedly reacting to truncation after the fact.

questions.topic: Output Truncation and Token Limits
questions.question: What is a practical sign that a task should be planned in sections from the start, rather than attempted as one large request?

options.A: Past experience or the nature of the request suggests the full desired output is likely to be very long relative to typical response length
options.B: The task is very short and simple
options.C: The task has no relationship to length considerations
options.D: The request involves fewer than ten words

questions.explanation: Anticipating a very long output based on the nature or past experience of similar requests is the practical cue for proactive sectioning.

questions.topic: Output Truncation and Token Limits
questions.question: After receiving a continued response following truncation, a user notices a sentence appears to be duplicated across the boundary. What is the appropriate fix?

options.A: Discard the entire response and start over from nothing
options.B: Leave the duplication in place since it's a minor issue
options.C: Assume duplication at boundaries can never be fixed
options.D: Edit out the duplicated content at the boundary so the combined text reads as a single coherent passage

questions.explanation: A quick manual edit at the boundary is a proportionate fix for the occasional duplication that can occur when stitching together a continued response.

questions.topic: Output Truncation and Token Limits
questions.question: Why is recognizing truncation (versus assuming a response is simply complete) an important troubleshooting skill?

options.A: This skill is only relevant for very technical tasks
options.B: Recognizing truncation has no practical consequence either way
options.C: A trailing incomplete sentence or cut-off list can be mistaken for a complete response if not specifically checked for, leading to an unknowingly incomplete deliverable
options.D: Truncation is always obvious and requires no particular skill to recognize

questions.explanation: An unnoticed truncated response risks being used as if it were complete, so recognizing the signs is a practically important check.

questions.topic: Document Chunking for Oversized Input Files
questions.question: A user needs to compare information from the beginning and end of a very large document that had to be chunked separately. What is a reasonable approach?

options.A: Combine the chunks back into their original unchunked form with no analysis
options.B: Only ever look at the first chunk and ignore the rest entirely
options.C: Assume the comparison is impossible once the document has been chunked
options.D: Extract the relevant specific details from each relevant chunk's analysis and explicitly compare them in a follow-up synthesis step

questions.explanation: A dedicated synthesis step that explicitly pulls together relevant details from different chunks is the practical way to make cross-chunk comparisons.

questions.topic: Document Chunking for Oversized Input Files
questions.question: What is a reasonable way to decide how large each chunk of a document should be when splitting it for processing?

options.A: Chunk size is irrelevant and can be chosen completely at random
options.B: Always use exactly the same fixed chunk size regardless of the document's actual structure
options.C: Balance chunk size against practical processing limits and the need to preserve coherent, meaningful sections rather than splitting arbitrarily
options.D: Always split into the smallest possible chunks regardless of content

questions.explanation: Balancing practical size limits against preserving coherent sections is the sound basis for choosing chunk boundaries.

questions.topic: Document Chunking for Oversized Input Files
questions.question: A user chunks a long contract into sections by page number, splitting some clauses mid-sentence across chunk boundaries. What problem does this risk creating?

options.A: No problem; page-based splitting is always the most reliable method
options.B: A clause split mid-sentence across chunks may be misinterpreted or evaluated incompletely within a single chunk, since a chunk-level analysis wouldn't see the clause's full text together
options.C: This approach guarantees a more accurate analysis than splitting by logical section
options.D: Contracts can never be meaningfully chunked under any method

questions.explanation: Splitting by an arbitrary boundary like page number, rather than logical structure like clauses, risks breaking up meaningful units of text mid-analysis.

questions.topic: Document Chunking for Oversized Input Files
questions.question: Why might it help to briefly restate key relevant context from a previous chunk when processing the next chunk in sequence?

options.A: This technique is only relevant for numerical documents
options.B: This is never helpful and always wastes effort
options.C: Restating context always introduces new errors with no benefit
options.D: It gives the next chunk's processing step some continuity with what came before, reducing the risk of losing important cross-chunk connections

questions.explanation: Brief continuity context bridges the gap between chunks, helping preserve connections that a strict, isolated chunk-by-chunk approach might otherwise lose.

questions.topic: Escaping Repetitive and Formulaic Output
questions.question: A user has tried varying the prompt wording several times but keeps getting essentially the same structure back. What is another lever to try?

options.A: Reduce the request to a single word with no further detail
options.B: Repeat the exact same wording one more time and expect a different result
options.C: Try a substantially different framing altogether — such as a different persona, a constraint that forces a new angle, or breaking the request into a different sequence of sub-steps
options.D: Give up on achieving variation entirely

questions.explanation: When minor wording tweaks aren't enough, a more substantial change in framing, persona, or constraints is the next lever to try for genuine variation.

questions.topic: Escaping Repetitive and Formulaic Output
questions.question: Why might explicitly forbidding a specific overused phrase or structure help reduce formulaic output?

options.A: This technique never has any effect on output
options.B: Directly ruling out the specific pattern that's been recurring removes the 'default' option, pushing toward a genuinely different response
options.C: Forbidding phrases always makes output worse with no benefit
options.D: This technique only works for numerical content

questions.explanation: Explicitly ruling out the recurring pattern removes the path of least resistance, encouraging a genuinely different response.

questions.topic: Escaping Repetitive and Formulaic Output
questions.question: A user wants Claude to avoid the very common opening structure of yet another business email starting with 'I hope this email finds you well.' What is a direct fix?

options.A: Accept the repeated opening as unavoidable
options.B: Explicitly instruct Claude to skip that specific stock opening and start with something more direct or specific to the situation
options.C: Rewrite only the closing while leaving the flagged opening untouched
options.D: Assume no instruction can influence this specific pattern

questions.explanation: Directly naming the specific pattern to avoid is the most reliable lever for eliminating it, especially for well-known, extremely common stock phrasings.

questions.topic: Fixing Formatting Problems in Output
questions.question: A user needs headers in a document to follow a specific numbering convention (e.g., 1.1, 1.2, 2.1) that the first draft didn't use. What is the direct fix?

options.A: Explicitly request the specific numbering convention needed, giving a short example if helpful, and ask for the headers to be reformatted accordingly
options.B: Accept the draft's existing header style with no changes
options.C: Assume numbering conventions can never be applied to headers
options.D: Remove all headers from the document entirely

questions.explanation: Explicitly specifying the exact convention (with an example if useful) is the direct way to get headers reformatted to match a specific numbering style.

questions.topic: Fixing Formatting Problems in Output
questions.question: Why can showing a small example of the exact desired formatting be more effective than describing it only in words?

options.A: Examples are never more effective than word descriptions for formatting
options.B: There is no meaningful difference between the two approaches for formatting
options.C: Examples can only be used for content, never for formatting
options.D: A concrete example removes ambiguity about exactly what the described formatting rule means in practice, similar to how examples help with style-matching more generally

questions.explanation: Just as with style-matching, a concrete formatting example resolves ambiguity that a purely verbal description might leave open.

questions.topic: Resolving Conflicting Instructions (User Prompt vs. Project Instructions)
questions.question: A user finds that a specific request in a conversation and a Project's standing instruction give genuinely opposite guidance on an important point (not just a minor style preference). What is the most careful approach?

options.A: Assume one instruction is automatically and always correct with no further thought
options.B: Ignore both instructions and proceed with neither
options.C: Pause to explicitly clarify which should apply in this case, since a genuine substantive conflict (not just style) deserves deliberate resolution rather than a default assumption
options.D: Delete the Project immediately without resolving the specific conflict

questions.explanation: A substantive conflict — as opposed to a minor style question — deserves explicit clarification rather than an unexamined default assumption.

questions.topic: Resolving Conflicting Instructions (User Prompt vs. Project Instructions)
questions.question: What is a reasonable way to prevent conflicting instructions from arising in the first place, rather than only resolving them after the fact?

options.A: Add new instructions freely with no consideration of how they interact with existing ones
options.B: Prevention is unnecessary since conflicts never actually cause any real issues
options.C: Before adding a new standing instruction, briefly check it against existing ones for potential contradiction
options.D: Conflicting instructions can never be prevented under any circumstances

questions.explanation: A brief consistency check before adding new standing instructions is a practical way to prevent conflicts from accumulating in the first place.

questions.topic: Claude Model Tiers for Business Tasks
questions.question: A user runs the same moderately complex task on two different tiers and finds the faster tier's output is indistinguishable in quality for their purposes. What is a reasonable conclusion?

options.A: The faster tier is likely a suitable, more cost-effective choice for this specific task going forward
options.B: The comparison is meaningless and should be ignored
options.C: The slower, more expensive tier should always be used regardless of this finding
options.D: Quality can never actually be compared across tiers

questions.explanation: An empirical head-to-head comparison showing equivalent quality is exactly the evidence needed to justify standardizing on the more cost-effective tier for that task.

questions.topic: Claude Product Surfaces (Chat, Projects, Artifacts, Research Mode)
questions.question: What is a sound way to think about the relationship between Projects and Artifacts as product surfaces?

options.A: Artifacts always replace the need for Projects entirely
options.B: They are mutually exclusive and can never be used for related work
options.C: A Project can provide the persistent context for an ongoing body of work, within which individual Artifacts can hold specific substantial deliverables produced along the way
options.D: Projects always replace the need for Artifacts entirely

questions.explanation: Projects and Artifacts serve complementary roles — persistent context versus specific standalone deliverables — and are often used together.

questions.topic: Choosing the Right Feature for a Task
questions.question: A user is uncertain whether a task needs a research/search-enabled mode. What is a reasonable test question?

options.A: Does the request contain the word 'the'?
options.B: Is the task written in complete sentences?
options.C: Is the request longer than one paragraph?
options.D: Does the task depend on any fact that could have changed recently, or that requires up-to-the-moment information?

questions.explanation: Whether the task genuinely depends on current or recently-changing information is the substantive test for needing a search-enabled mode.

questions.topic: Claude Plans and Business Deployment Considerations
questions.question: Why might a growing business periodically revisit its choice of Claude plan/deployment rather than treating the initial choice as permanent?

options.A: Plan choice should never be revisited once made
options.B: As team size, collaboration needs, and governance requirements evolve, a previously suitable plan may no longer be the best fit, warranting periodic reassessment
options.C: Revisiting plan choice always causes disruption with no benefit
options.D: Plan/deployment choice has no relationship to a business's evolving needs

questions.explanation: Evolving organizational needs are a legitimate reason to periodically reassess whether the current plan/deployment still fits, rather than treating the initial choice as permanent.

questions.topic: Claude Projects Setup and Custom Instructions
questions.question: A Project is used by multiple people who each have slightly different preferences for a minor stylistic detail. How should this generally be handled?

options.A: Every individual preference must be permanently encoded into the standing Project instructions with no exceptions
options.B: Shared Projects can never accommodate any individual variation
options.C: Standing instructions should be left blank whenever more than one person uses a Project
options.D: The Project's standing instructions should capture the shared, agreed-upon baseline, with individuals able to state specific personal preferences within their own individual conversations as needed

questions.explanation: A shared baseline at the Project level, with room for individual, conversation-specific adjustments, reasonably balances consistency and personal preference.

questions.topic: Claude Projects Setup and Custom Instructions
questions.question: What is a reasonable check to include when reviewing a Project's custom instructions for quality?

options.A: Whether the instructions are written in the longest possible sentences
options.B: Whether the instructions include as many unrelated topics as possible
options.C: Whether each instruction is clear, specific, and actually reflects a genuine standing need rather than a one-off preference
options.D: Whether the instructions avoid mentioning tone or format entirely

questions.explanation: Clarity, specificity, and genuine standing relevance are the practical quality markers for custom instructions, mirroring good prompt-writing principles.

questions.topic: Knowledge Source Configuration
questions.question: A Project's knowledge sources have grown over time to include many documents, some no longer relevant to current work. What is a reasonable maintenance step?

options.A: Delete the entire Project rather than reviewing individual sources
options.B: Add even more unrelated documents to compensate for the growth
options.C: Periodically review the knowledge sources and remove or archive ones that are no longer relevant to the Project's current purpose
options.D: Never review or remove any knowledge source once added, regardless of continued relevance

questions.explanation: Periodic pruning of outdated or irrelevant knowledge sources keeps a Project's grounding material relevant and focused over time.

questions.topic: Knowledge Source Configuration
questions.question: Why is it useful to consider the format and clarity of a document before adding it as a knowledge source, not just its topical relevance?

options.A: A topically relevant but poorly organized or unclear document may be harder to draw accurate, well-grounded information from than a clearer one
options.B: Clarity only matters for documents that will never actually be referenced
options.C: Only the file size of a document matters for its usefulness as a knowledge source
options.D: Format and clarity never affect how useful a knowledge source actually is

questions.explanation: Clarity and organization affect how reliably relevant information can actually be drawn from a document, not just whether the topic is a match.

questions.topic: Custom Instructions Scope and Precedence
questions.question: A user wants to understand why a particular formatting preference applied in one conversation but not in a different, seemingly similar one within the same Project. What is a likely explanation to check first?

options.A: This kind of inconsistency is unexplainable and cannot be investigated
options.B: All conversations within the same Project are always identical in every respect
options.C: Projects apply instructions completely randomly with no discoverable pattern
options.D: The preference was likely stated as a one-off request in the first conversation rather than saved as a Project-level instruction, so it didn't carry over automatically

questions.explanation: Checking whether the preference was a one-off in-conversation request (versus a persisted Project-level instruction) is the most likely, checkable explanation.

questions.topic: Custom Instructions Scope and Precedence
questions.question: What is a reasonable general rule of thumb for the scope of an instruction relative to how often it should apply?

options.A: Scope has no bearing on where an instruction should reasonably be placed
options.B: All instructions should always be placed at the Project level regardless of how narrowly they apply
options.C: Instructions meant to apply broadly and consistently belong at the Project level; instructions relevant to only a single specific request belong in that individual conversation
options.D: All instructions should always be placed within individual conversations regardless of how broadly they apply

questions.explanation: Matching instruction placement to its intended breadth of application — broad and recurring at the Project level, narrow and one-off within a conversation — is the sound rule of thumb.

questions.topic: Organizing Projects for Teams
questions.question: A company is deciding between one large Project per department versus many small Projects per individual initiative. What is a reasonable factor in this decision?

options.A: Larger Projects are always better regardless of how distinct the underlying initiatives are
options.B: This decision should be made with no consideration of actual context overlap
options.C: The number of letters in the department's name
options.D: Whether initiatives within a department share enough common context/instructions to benefit from being grouped together, versus being distinct enough to warrant separate configuration

questions.explanation: The degree of genuine shared context between initiatives is the substantive factor in deciding Project granularity, not arbitrary factors like naming.

questions.topic: Organizing Projects for Teams
questions.question: Why might overly fragmented Projects (many very narrow, single-purpose Projects with heavy overlap) create their own inefficiency?

options.A: Fragmentation never creates any inefficiency regardless of degree
options.B: Excessive fragmentation can lead to duplicated configuration effort and confusion about which nearly-identical Project to use for a given task
options.C: More Projects always means better organization with no downside
options.D: Fragmentation is only a concern for very small organizations

questions.explanation: Excessive fragmentation trades one problem (an overly broad Project) for another (duplicated setup and confusion among many overlapping narrow ones).

questions.topic: Organizing Projects for Teams
questions.question: A team wants to standardize how new Projects are set up going forward (e.g., a checklist for instructions and knowledge sources to consider). What is the benefit of this practice?

options.A: Standardization always makes Project setup worse
options.B: No benefit; every new Project should be configured with no reference to prior practice
options.C: This practice is only relevant for organizations with a single Project
options.D: A standard setup checklist helps ensure new Projects are configured thoughtfully and consistently, reducing the chance of missing important context or knowledge sources

questions.explanation: A consistent setup checklist reduces the chance of overlooking important configuration and promotes consistency across a team's Projects.

questions.topic: Recognizing When Human Review or Escalation Is Required
questions.question: A recurring low-stakes task occasionally surfaces genuinely high-stakes edge cases mixed in with routine ones. What is a reasonable design for handling this?

options.A: Escalate every single instance, including the routine ones, with no differentiation
options.B: Ignore the existence of high-stakes edge cases entirely since they're infrequent
options.C: Treat every instance identically as low-stakes with no differentiation
options.D: Build in a way to identify and flag the high-stakes edge cases specifically for escalation, while continuing to handle the genuinely routine cases with lighter-touch review

questions.explanation: Differentiating and specifically flagging the high-stakes edge cases for escalation — while keeping routine handling lightweight — is a proportionate design.

questions.topic: Risk Categorization for High-Stakes Outputs
questions.question: A piece of content is low-risk in isolation but will be combined with several other pieces into a single high-stakes public report. How should the individual piece be treated?

options.A: Combined use never changes the appropriate risk treatment of an individual component
options.B: It should always be treated as low-risk regardless of how it will ultimately be used
options.C: Only the final combined report needs any review; individual components never do
options.D: Its treatment should reflect the risk of its ultimate combined use in the high-stakes report, warranting more careful review than its standalone content might otherwise suggest

questions.explanation: Risk categorization should account for a component's ultimate use — a low-risk-seeming piece feeding into a high-stakes final product warrants review calibrated to that eventual use.

questions.topic: Organizational Policy Compliance for AI Use
questions.question: What is a reasonable approach when an organization's AI policy hasn't yet been updated to address a genuinely new type of use case?

options.A: Assume policies never need to be updated once written
options.B: Avoid ever raising the gap with anyone
options.C: Treat the gap as a prompt to seek guidance from an appropriate internal contact, and suggest the policy be updated to explicitly address the new use case going forward
options.D: Assume the new use case is automatically approved since it isn't explicitly addressed

questions.explanation: Proactively seeking guidance and flagging the policy gap is more responsible than assuming automatic approval for an unaddressed new use case.

questions.topic: Output Truncation and Token Limits
questions.question: A recurring monthly report reliably runs long enough to risk truncation. What is a durable process fix?

options.A: Continue generating it as one large request every month and manually asking to continue each time with no planning
options.B: Stop producing the monthly report altogether
options.C: Build the report generation process around a planned, sectioned approach from the start, given the known, predictable length
options.D: Randomly shorten the report's actual content every month with no relation to its real scope

questions.explanation: Since the length pattern is known and predictable for this recurring report, planning a sectioned approach from the outset is more durable than repeatedly reacting after each truncation.

questions.topic: Output Truncation and Token Limits
questions.question: What is a reasonable way to estimate whether a requested deliverable is at meaningful risk of truncation before starting?

options.A: Consider the scope and detail level requested (e.g., number of sections, depth of detail) relative to what similar past requests have needed, and section the work proactively if the scope looks large
options.B: Assume every request, regardless of scope, carries identical truncation risk
options.C: Only requests containing images ever carry truncation risk
options.D: Length risk can never be reasonably estimated in advance

questions.explanation: Comparing the requested scope/detail against what similar past requests have needed is a practical way to anticipate and proactively manage truncation risk.

questions.topic: Document Chunking for Oversized Input Files
questions.question: A user repeatedly needs to analyze similarly-structured large documents (e.g., monthly reports of a consistent format). What is an efficient chunking approach?

options.A: Chunk each document into a random number of arbitrarily-sized pieces every time
options.B: Re-derive a completely new, ad hoc chunking strategy from scratch every single time with no reuse of past approach
options.C: Develop a consistent chunking approach based on the documents' shared, predictable structure, and reuse that approach each time this type of document needs processing
options.D: Avoid chunking these documents under any circumstances

questions.explanation: A reusable, structure-aware chunking approach is more efficient for recurring, similarly-structured documents than reinventing the strategy each time.

questions.topic: Document Chunking for Oversized Input Files
questions.question: Why might chunking strategy need to differ between a document with clear section headers versus one that is one long undifferentiated block of text?

options.A: Chunking strategy should always be identical regardless of a document's internal structure
options.B: A document with clear headers offers natural, meaningful split points, while an undifferentiated block requires more careful judgment to find reasonable break points that preserve coherent meaning
options.C: Undifferentiated documents can never be chunked under any approach
options.D: Documents with headers should never be chunked at all

questions.explanation: The presence or absence of natural structural markers directly affects how straightforward it is to find coherent, meaning-preserving chunk boundaries.

questions.topic: Escaping Repetitive and Formulaic Output
questions.question: A user wants variety across a batch of similar short pieces of content (e.g., ten product taglines) generated in a single request. What is a useful technique?

options.A: Provide no guidance at all and hope for natural variation across all ten
options.B: Request all ten with completely identical instructions and no differentiation between them
options.C: Explicitly assign a different constraint, angle, or tone to each of the ten within the same request, so each one is prompted toward a genuinely different result
options.D: Request only one tagline and duplicate it ten times

questions.explanation: Explicitly differentiating the angle or constraint for each item within a single batch request is a direct way to engineer genuine variety across the set.

questions.topic: Escaping Repetitive and Formulaic Output
questions.question: What is a limitation of relying purely on asking for 'more creativity' to fix repetitive output, without any more specific guidance?

options.A: This approach always works perfectly with no limitation
options.B: Asking for creativity is the only approach that could ever work
options.C: A vague request for 'more creativity' gives no concrete direction, and may not reliably break a specific recurring pattern the way a more targeted change (persona, angle, explicit constraint) would
options.D: This limitation applies only to numerical content

questions.explanation: Vague requests for 'more creativity' lack the concrete, actionable specificity that a targeted change in framing or constraint provides.

questions.topic: Fixing Formatting Problems in Output
questions.question: A response uses inconsistent heading levels (e.g., jumping from a top-level heading directly to a deeply nested one with no intermediate levels). What is the appropriate fix?

options.A: Assume heading hierarchy can never be corrected
options.B: Accept the inconsistent heading structure since the content itself is accurate
options.C: Ask for the heading hierarchy to be corrected to a consistent, logical structure with appropriate intermediate levels
options.D: Remove all headings from the document entirely

questions.explanation: A direct request to fix the heading hierarchy into a logical, consistent structure is the straightforward fix for this kind of formatting problem.

questions.topic: Fixing Formatting Problems in Output
questions.question: Why is it useful to check formatting against the actual destination (e.g., a specific document template or platform) rather than judging it in isolation?

options.A: Formatting that looks fine in isolation may still not match the specific conventions or constraints of where it will actually be used, so checking against the real destination catches mismatches isolated review would miss
options.B: Destination-specific formatting requirements never matter
options.C: This consideration is only relevant for coding-related content
options.D: All destinations always accept identical formatting with no meaningful differences

questions.explanation: Destination-specific conventions can differ from generic 'good formatting,' so checking against the actual target catches mismatches that isolated review wouldn't surface.

questions.topic: Resolving Conflicting Instructions (User Prompt vs. Project Instructions)
questions.question: A newly added Project instruction unintentionally contradicts a long-standing one that most users still expect to be in effect. What is a reasonable way to handle the transition?

options.A: Make the change silently with no communication to Project users
options.B: Communicate the change clearly to people who use the Project, and consider explicitly removing or updating the outdated instruction rather than leaving both in an unresolved contradictory state
options.C: Leave both contradictory instructions in place indefinitely with no communication
options.D: Delete the entire Project rather than resolving the specific contradiction

questions.explanation: Clear communication plus explicit resolution of the outdated instruction addresses both the practical contradiction and the risk of confusing existing users.

questions.topic: Output Truncation and Token Limits
questions.question: A user is midway through a very long generated list when it cuts off. Before asking Claude to continue, what is a useful quick check?

options.A: Note exactly where the content stopped, so the continuation can be checked for a clean, non-duplicated pickup at that precise point
options.B: There is no need to note where it stopped; continuations are always seamless with no verification needed
options.C: Assume the entire list must be regenerated from the very beginning
options.D: Assume the cutoff means the topic cannot be discussed further

questions.explanation: Noting the exact stopping point makes it easy to verify the continuation picks up cleanly, without gaps or duplication at the seam.

questions.topic: Resolving Conflicting Instructions (User Prompt vs. Project Instructions)
questions.question: Which best summarizes a sound overall approach to conflicting instructions across scopes (Project-level vs. conversation-specific)?

options.A: Always assume conflicts are impossible and never check for them
options.B: Always delete all instructions at every level whenever any conflict is noticed
options.C: Notice the conflict, resolve it deliberately for the case at hand, and update the standing configuration if the conflict reveals the default itself needs to change
options.D: Always let the most recently typed instruction silently override everything with no further thought

questions.explanation: Deliberate noticing, resolving, and — where warranted — updating the standing default is the sound general pattern for handling instruction conflicts across scopes.
